subject: surgery
title: Orbital Blowout Fractures, Facial Nerve Injury, and Maxillofacial Airway

steps.tx: Direct impact from a blunt object larger than the orbital aperture transmits sudden hydraulic pressure through the globe and orbital soft tissues. This force causes fracture of the fragile bony walls while preserving the thick orbital rim, a condition termed an **orbital blowout fracture**. The thin bone of the orbital floor medial to the infraorbital canal and the paper-thin lamina papyracea of the medial ethmoid wall are the most vulnerable sites of collapse.
steps.say: Blunt objects larger than the orbital opening drive hydraulic pressure through the globe. This sudden pressure blows out the thin orbital floor and medial lamina papyracea while leaving the orbital rim intact.

vis.alt: Anatomical skull illustration displaying orbital blowout fracture and midfacial fracture lines.
vis.caption: Orbital blowout fracture: downward herniation of orbital contents through the fractured maxillary floor. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Herniation of periorbital fat and the inferior rectus muscle into the maxillary sinus leads to tethering of the ocular globe. Clinically, patients present with painful vertical diplopia on upward gaze, enophthalmos, and hypoesthesia of the ipsilateral cheek and upper lip from traction on the **infraorbital nerve**. The forced duction test mechanically distinguishes true muscular entrapment from periorbital nerve palsy or soft tissue edema.
steps.say: Entrapment of the inferior rectus muscle causes upward gaze restriction and double vision. Injury to the infraorbital nerve creates cheek numbness, while the forced duction test confirms mechanical muscle tethering.

left.title: Mechanical Muscle Entrapment
points: Inferior rectus herniation into maxillary sinus
Marked limitation of upward and downward gaze
Positive forced duction test on forceps traction
Surgical release within two weeks recommended

right.title: Neurogenic Ocular Paresis
points: Negative forced duction test with free globe rotation

steps.tx: Definitive surgical indications for orbital floor repair include persistent disabling diplopia with confirmed rectus muscle entrapment, enophthalmos exceeding two millimetres, and a large bony floor defect greater than fifty percent. Access to the orbital floor is achieved via a **subciliary incision** or a scarless transconjunctival approach. Herniated orbital contents are gently elevated and the structural defect is reconstituted with titanium mesh or porous polyethylene implants.
steps.say: Surgical repair is indicated for muscle entrapment, marked enophthalmos, or large floor fractures. Surgeons elevate herniated tissue through a subciliary or transconjunctival incision and reconstruct the floor with synthetic mesh.

rows: Preseptal or postseptal through inferior fornix
Hidden conjunctival scar, minimal ectropion risk, requires lateral canthotomy
Stepped skin-muscle flap below lower lash line
Superb anterior and posterior floor exposure, higher risk of temporary ectropion
Allows packing support from below, poor superior visualization of trapped nerve

steps.tx: Temporal bone trauma produces peripheral facial paralysis through contusion, edema, or complete neural transection. Based on the relation of the fracture line to the long axis of the petrous pyramid, clinicians distinguish longitudinal fractures from **transverse temporal fracture** configurations. Transverse fractures run perpendicular to the petrous ridge, cause immediate facial nerve transection in up to fifty percent of cases, and frequently cause profound sensorineural hearing loss and severe vertigo.
steps.say: Transverse temporal bone fractures cross perpendicular to the petrous ridge. They carry a fifty percent risk of immediate facial nerve transection, severe vertigo, and permanent sensorineural hearing loss.

left.title: Longitudinal Temporal Fracture
points: Parallel to petrous ridge from lateral blunt blow
Accounts for eighty percent of all temporal fractures
Facial nerve paralysis occurs in twenty percent
Delayed onset paralysis from nerve edema
Conductive hearing loss from ossicular disruption

right.title: Transverse Temporal Fracture
points: Perpendicular to petrous ridge from frontal or occipital blow
Accounts for twenty percent of temporal bone fractures
Facial nerve paralysis occurs in fifty percent
Immediate complete paralysis from nerve transection
Profound sensorineural deafness and vestibular destruction

steps.tx: Assessing facial nerve recovery following acute maxillofacial trauma requires standardized clinical staging and serial electrodiagnostic testing. Functional impairment is documented using the **House-Brackmann scale**, which grades facial motor function from grade one representing normal symmetry to grade six denoting complete flaccid paralysis. Electroneuronography showing greater than ninety percent axonal degeneration within fourteen days of injury represents a classic indication for surgical facial nerve decompression.
steps.say: The House-Brackmann scale grades facial nerve motor deficits from normal tone to flaccid paralysis. Electroneuronography showing over ninety percent degeneration within two weeks warrants surgical nerve decompression.

vis.alt: Medical diagram illustrating facial nerve motor innervation and peripheral versus central facial paralysis.
vis.caption: Facial nerve motor evaluation: peripheral lower motor neuron injury causing ipsilateral forehead and lower facial paralysis. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Lacerations across the lateral cheek crossing an imaginary line between the tragus and the upper lip carry a high risk of direct facial nerve division. When transection occurs, primary **epineural repair** using fine nine-zero or ten-zero monofilament nylon sutures under operating microscope magnification yields optimal axonal regeneration. When segmental nerve loss precludes tension-free end-to-end coaptation, a cable graft harvested from the sural nerve or great auricular nerve is interposed.
steps.say: Deep cheek lacerations may divide the facial nerve trunk or branches. Tension-free epineural repair under the microscope restores continuity, while cable nerve grafts bridge larger gaps.

steps.tx: Severe maxillofacial trauma precipitates acute, catastrophic airway obstruction from multiple synergistic mechanisms. In comminuted symphyseal or bilateral parasymphyseal mandibular fractures, detachment of the genioglossus and geniohyoid musculature results in **flail mandible**, allowing the tongue base to collapse backward into the hypopharynx. Massive intraoral bleeding, avulsed loose teeth, expanding pharyngeal hematomas, and rapid soft tissue edema compound this acute obstruction, demanding immediate emergency positioning and intervention.
steps.say: Bilateral anterior mandibular fractures detach the muscles supporting the tongue base, causing the tongue to collapse backward into the hypopharynx. Traumatic intraoral hemorrhage and mucosal edema quickly precipitate complete suffocation.

rows: Loss of genioglossus tongue support and posterior airway prolapse
Manual anterior tongue traction with clamp or suture, jaw-thrust maneuver
Copious pooling of blood into hypopharynx and larynx
Rigid Yankauer suction, anterior and posterior nasopharyngeal pack
Downward and backward displacement of maxilla against pharynx
Digital disimpaction and manual anterior repositioning of upper jaw

steps.tx: When severe panfacial trauma, crushed facial bones, and massive hemorrhage render bag-valve-mask ventilation impossible and prevent visualization during endotracheal intubation, a definitive surgical airway is mandatory. In the acute resuscitation bay, an emergency **surgical cricothyroidotomy** through the cricothyroid membrane provides rapid, lifesaving subglottic ventilation. Once initial hemorrhage and facial reconstruction stabilize, the temporary cricothyroidotomy tube is converted to an elective formal tracheostomy to prevent long-term subglottic stenosis.
steps.say: When massive facial destruction prevents oral intubation, surgical cricothyroidotomy provides immediate lifesaving ventilation through the cricothyroid membrane. This is converted to formal tracheostomy once stabilized.
